items.title: Languages, Scripts and Classical Languages
items.body:
### Languages, scripts and classical status

**In one line**
Indian languages belong to four families, descend from a few ancient scripts, and some are given special 'classical language' status by the government.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC asks the family of a language, the earliest script and its direction, and the year a language (especially Telugu) became classical.

**The story**
Most north-Indian speech grew from Sanskrit through Prakrit and Pali; the four big southern tongues form a separate Dravidian family; smaller families cover the Himalayas and tribal belts. All these were first written in **Brahmi**, the parent of nearly every later Indian script, while the north-west briefly used **Kharoshthi**, written the other way round. From 2004 the government began recognising languages of great antiquity and literary depth as 'classical'.

**Why it matters**
Classical status brings funding and prestige, and the recognition years (Tamil 2004, Telugu 2008) are frequently tested one-mark facts.

**Picture it**

| Language | Year |
|---|---|
| Tamil | 2004 |
| Sanskrit | 2005 |
| Telugu, Kannada | 2008 |
| Malayalam | 2013 |
| Odia | 2014 |
| Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese, Bengali | 2024 |

Families: Indo-Aryan (~74%), Dravidian (~25%; includes Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam), Sino-Tibetan, Austric (includes Santhali, Khasi and Nicobarese). Tamil is the oldest Dravidian language; Telugu is the largest. Scripts: Brahmi (left-to-right, parent), Kharoshthi/Kharosthi (right-to-left, Gandhara; used in the Ashokan edicts of the north-west), then Gupta → Nagari/Devanagari, Grantha, Tamil-Brahmi.

**Terms explained**
- **Language family** — a group of languages with a shared ancestor.
- **Script** — the set of letters used to write a language.
- **Classical language** — a status for tongues with ~1500–2000 years of age and rich literature.
- **Indo-Aryan / Dravidian** — the northern (Sanskrit-derived) and southern language groups.

**Don't confuse**
- **Brahmi vs Kharoshthi** — Brahmi runs left-to-right and is the parent script; Kharoshthi runs right-to-left and was limited to the north-west.
- **Oldest vs largest Dravidian** — Tamil is oldest; Telugu is largest. Do not swap.

**Remember it**
Tamil first (2004), Telugu with Kannada (2008) — 'Tamil leads, Telugu-Kannada follow four years later'.

**TL;DR**
- Four families: Indo-Aryan (~74%), Dravidian (~25%), Sino-Tibetan, Austric.
- Brahmi = earliest script (left-to-right), parent of most Indian scripts; Kharoshthi = right-to-left.
- Tamil (2004) = first classical language; Telugu & Kannada = 2008.
- 2024 additions: Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese, Bengali.
keyPoints: Four language families: Indo-Aryan (~74%), Dravidian (~25%), Sino-Tibetan, Austric
Tamil = oldest Dravidian language; Telugu = largest Dravidian language
Brahmi is the earliest Indian script (left-to-right); Kharosthi was written right-to-left
Brahmi is the parent script of Gupta → Nagari, Grantha and Tamil-Brahmi
Tamil (2004) was the first classical language; Telugu and Kannada both in 2008
2024 additions: Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali
Austric family includes Santhali, Khasi and Nicobarese; Kharosthi was used in Ashokan edicts of the north-west.

items.title: Streams of Indian Literature — Sangam, Persian and Telugu
items.body:
### Streams of Indian literature

**In one line**
India's classical literature flows in several streams — Tamil Sangam, Persian/Urdu and Telugu — each with signature works and authors.

**Why it is asked**
Match-the-following questions pair a work with its author or stream, and APPSC gives extra weight to the Telugu line.

**The story**
In the deep south, poets of the **Sangam** academies produced grammar, ethics and epic. After the 12th century, **Persian** became the court language and generated royal chronicles and memoirs, out of which **Urdu** later grew. In the Telugu country, three poets began a Telugu Mahabharata, and the tradition climbed to a golden age in the Vijayanagara court of Krishnadevaraya.

**Why it matters**
These works show how literature followed political power, and the Telugu stream is directly examinable AP heritage.

**Picture it**

| Stream | Signature works |
|---|---|
| Sangam (Tamil) | Tolkappiyam (grammar), Tirukkural (ethics), Silappadikaram & Manimekalai (twin epics) |
| Persian/Urdu | Akbarnama (Abul Fazl), Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi (Zia-ud-din Barani), Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (memoirs of Emperor Jahangir), Saare Jahan Se Achcha (Muhammad Iqbal) |
| Telugu | Andhra Mahabharatam (Kavitrayam), Amuktamalyada (Krishnadevaraya), Manucharitra (Peddana) |

**Sangam:** Tolkappiyam is the oldest Tamil grammar; the Tirukkural (Thiruvalluvar) has 1,330 couplets on ethics, polity and love; Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal) and Manimekalai (Sathanar) are the twin epics. **Persian/Urdu:** Amir Khusrau pioneered Indo-Persian poetry; Urdu grew from Persian vocabulary over Hindi grammar; Iqbal wrote Bang-i-Dara. **Telugu:** the Kavitrayam (Nannaya 'Adi Kavi', Tikkana, Yerrapragada) rendered the Andhra Mahabharatam; Pothana (Bhagavatam), Vemana (verse-aphorisms), the potter-poet Atukuri Molla (a Telugu Ramayana), and the Ashtadiggajas led by Allasani Peddana (Andhra Kavita Pitamaha) mark the golden age.

**Terms explained**
- **Sangam** — ancient Tamil poets' academies and their literature.
- **Couplet** — a pair of lines (the Tirukkural's form).
- **Prabandha** — a Telugu long narrative poem.
- **Ashtadiggajas** — the 'eight elephants', Krishnadevaraya's eight court poets.

**Don't confuse**
- **Silappadikaram vs Manimekalai** — both are twin epics; Silappadikaram is about Kannagi/justice, Manimekalai is its Buddhist sequel.
- **Kavitrayam vs Ashtadiggajas** — the Kavitrayam are the three Mahabharata poets; the Ashtadiggajas are the eight later Vijayanagara court poets.

**Remember it**
Telugu Mahabharata trio order 'NA-TI-E': Nannaya, Tikkana, Errana.

**TL;DR**
- Sangam: Tolkappiyam (grammar), Tirukkural (ethics), Silappadikaram + Manimekalai (twin epics).
- Persian: Akbarnama (Abul Fazl), Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi (Barani); Iqbal wrote Saare Jahan Se Achcha.
- Telugu Kavitrayam = Nannaya + Tikkana + Yerrapragada (Andhra Mahabharatam).
- Krishnadevaraya wrote Amuktamalyada; Peddana wrote Manucharitra.
keyPoints: Tolkappiyam is the oldest Tamil grammar; Tirukkural has 1,330 ethical couplets
Silappadikaram and Manimekalai are the twin Tamil epics
Persian was the court language from the 12th century; Amir Khusrau pioneered Indo-Persian poetry
Abul Fazl wrote Akbarnama; Barani wrote Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi
Iqbal wrote Saare Jahan Se Achcha and Bang-i-Dara (Urdu)
Telugu Kavitrayam = Nannaya, Tikkana, Yerrapragada (Andhra Mahabharatam)
Krishnadevaraya wrote Amuktamalyada; Ashtadiggajas led by Allasani Peddana ('Andhra Kavita Pitamaha', Manucharitra)
Atukuri Molla, a potter-poet, composed a Telugu Ramayana

items.title: Schools of Indian Philosophy (Darshanas)
items.body:
### Schools of Indian philosophy

**In one line**
Indian philosophy splits into six 'orthodox' schools that accept the Vedas and several 'heterodox' schools that reject them.

**Why it is asked**
A classic APPSC item asks which school is NOT orthodox, or matches a school to its founder/core idea.

**The story**
Thinkers who accepted the authority of the Vedas built six **orthodox (Astika)** systems, usually studied in three pairs. Thinkers who rejected Vedic authority formed **heterodox (Nastika)** schools — including the two great religions Buddhism and Jainism, the materialist Charvaka, the fatalist Ajivika, and the sceptical Ajnana. Within orthodox Vedanta, three sub-traditions argued over how the soul relates to Brahman.

**Why it matters**
These schools underlie Indian logic, science and religion, and the orthodox/heterodox split is a reliable discriminator question.

**Picture it**

| School | Founder | Core idea |
|---|---|---|
| Samkhya | Kapila | dualism of Purusha & Prakriti (oldest) |
| Yoga | Patanjali | Ashtanga path to liberation |
| Nyaya | Akshapada Gautama | logic & valid knowledge |
| Vaisheshika | Kanada | atomism (anu) & elements |
| Mimamsa | Jaimini | ritual/karma of the Vedas |
| Vedanta | Badarayana (Vyasa) | Brahman as ultimate reality |

Vedanta traditions: Advaita (Shankaracharya, non-dualism), Vishishtadvaita (Ramanuja, qualified non-dualism), Dvaita (Madhvacharya, dualism). Heterodox: Buddhism (Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path), Jainism (Mahavira — liberation through ahimsa and asceticism; Anekantavada, Syadvada), Charvaka/Lokayata (Brihaspati, materialism — only perception is valid knowledge), Ajivika (Makkhali Gosala, determinism/Niyati), Ajnana (Sanjaya Belatthiputta, scepticism/skepticism about certain knowledge).

**Terms explained**
- **Darshana** — a system of philosophy (literally 'vision').
- **Astika / Nastika** — schools that accept / reject Vedic authority.
- **Dualism** — the view that two separate realities exist (e.g. spirit and matter).
- **Anekantavada** — the Jain idea that truth has many sides.

**Don't confuse**
- **Charvaka vs Ajivika** — Charvaka (Brihaspati) is materialism; Ajivika (Makkhali Gosala) is strict determinism (Niyati).
- **Orthodox vs heterodox** — orthodox accept the Vedas (the six darshanas); Buddhism, Jainism and Charvaka reject them.

**Remember it**
Six orthodox pairs: 'Sa-Yo, Nya-Vai, Mi-Ve' (Samkhya-Yoga, Nyaya-Vaisheshika, Mimamsa-Vedanta).

**TL;DR**
- Six orthodox (Shad Darshana): Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa, Vedanta.
- Samkhya (Kapila) is the oldest; Vedanta splits into Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, Dvaita.
- Heterodox reject the Vedas: Buddhism, Jainism, Charvaka, Ajivika, Ajnana.
- Charvaka = materialism; Ajivika = determinism.
keyPoints: Six orthodox schools (Shad Darshana): Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa, Vedanta
Samkhya (Kapila) is the oldest school — dualism of Purusha and Prakriti
Vedanta traditions: Advaita (Shankara), Vishishtadvaita (Ramanuja), Dvaita (Madhva)
Heterodox schools reject Vedic authority: Buddhism, Jainism, Charvaka, Ajivika, Ajnana
Charvaka (Brihaspati) = materialism; Ajivika (Makkhali Gosala) = determinism (Niyati)
Jain doctrines: Anekantavada (many-sidedness) and Syadvada (conditional predication)

items.title: The Eight Classical Dances
items.body:
### The eight classical dances

**In one line**
India has eight classical dances recognised by the Sangeet Natak Akademi, all built on one ancient treatise, the Natya Shastra.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC asks the count (eight), the home state of each form, and the Natya Shastra concepts (Tandava/Lasya, Nritta/Nritya/Natya).

**The story**
Every classical dance traces its grammar to Bharata Muni's **Natya Shastra**. It describes two moods — vigorous **Tandava** and graceful **Lasya** — and three ways of dancing: pure movement (**Nritta**), expressive storytelling (**Nritya**) and full drama (**Natya**). Over centuries each region refined its own form, so the Akademi recognises eight; the Ministry of Culture adds Chhau to make nine.

**Why it matters**
The home-state matching is a common one-mark question, and Kuchipudi marks Andhra's place in this national list.

**Picture it**

| Dance | State | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Bharatanatyam | Tamil Nadu | Devadasi origin; Carnatic music |
| Kuchipudi | Andhra Pradesh | dance-drama; Tarangam (plate dance) |
| Kathak | North India | 'Katha'/storytelling; Hindustani |
| Kathakali | Kerala | dance-drama, elaborate make-up, all-male |
| Mohiniyattam | Kerala | Lasya, solo female |
| Odissi | Odisha | 'mobile sculpture'; Gita Govinda |
| Manipuri | Manipur | Vaishnavite Raslila; soft movements |
| Sattriya | Assam | Sankardev; Vaishnavite monasteries |

Emotion is conveyed by nine rasas and 108 mudras.

**Terms explained**
- **Natya Shastra** — the ancient treatise (Bharata Muni) that defines dance and drama.
- **Tandava / Lasya** — the vigorous (masculine) and graceful (feminine) moods.
- **Nritta / Nritya / Natya** — pure dance / expressive dance / dramatic dance.
- **Mudra** — a symbolic hand gesture; **rasa** — an emotional flavour.

**Don't confuse**
- **Kathak vs Kathakali** — Kathak is the North Indian storytelling dance; Kathakali is the Kerala dance-drama with heavy make-up.
- **Kathakali vs Mohiniyattam** — both from Kerala, but Kathakali is vigorous dance-drama while Mohiniyattam is graceful solo Lasya.

**Remember it**
Two Kerala forms = Kathakali (drama) + Mohiniyattam (Lasya); Sattriya is the Assam one by Sankardev.

**TL;DR**
- All classical dance rests on Bharata Muni's Natya Shastra.
- Tandava (vigorous) vs Lasya (graceful); Nritta/Nritya/Natya; 9 rasas, 108 mudras.
- Eight SNA forms; Ministry of Culture adds Chhau (nine).
- Kuchipudi = Andhra Pradesh; Sattriya = Assam; Odissi = Odisha.
keyPoints: Classical dance is based on Bharata Muni's Natya Shastra
Tandava = masculine/vigorous; Lasya = feminine/graceful
Nritta (pure) / Nritya (expressive) / Natya (dramatic); nine rasas, 108 mudras
Sangeet Natak Akademi recognises 8 classical dances; Ministry of Culture adds Chhau (9)
Kerala has two forms: Kathakali (dance-drama) and Mohiniyattam (Lasya)
Sattriya (Assam) was introduced by Srimanta Sankardev; Odissi is called 'mobile sculpture'

items.title: Kuchipudi and Indian Classical Music
items.body:
### Kuchipudi and Indian classical music

**In one line**
Kuchipudi is Andhra Pradesh's classical dance-drama, and Indian classical music divides into northern Hindustani and southern Carnatic systems.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC tests Kuchipudi's codifier and signature item, and the Carnatic Trinity and Hindustani gharanas.

**The story**
**Kuchipudi** takes its name from a village in Andhra Pradesh, where it grew as a dance-drama performed by male-Brahmin *Bhagavathalu*. The saint **Siddhendra Yogi** shaped it into classical form with his *Bhamakalapam*. Indian classical **music** meanwhile split into two systems that share ragas and talas but differ in style: the northern Hindustani and the southern Carnatic, the latter sung across the Telugu and Tamil south.

**Why it matters**
Kuchipudi and Carnatic music are both strongly AP-linked, and the Trinity/gharana facts are standard one-mark items.

**Picture it**

| System | Region | Key names |
|---|---|---|
| Hindustani | North | gharanas: Gwalior (oldest), Kirana, Agra, Jaipur, Patiala |
| Carnatic | South (incl. AP) | Trinity: Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, Shyama Shastri |

Kuchipudi was popularised by Vempati Chinna Satyam and Raja & Radha Reddy; its *Tarangam* is footwork on the rim of a brass plate, and it uses *Vachika Abhinaya* (spoken/sung dialogue), set to Carnatic music with Telugu/Sanskrit lyrics. **M.S. Subbulakshmi** was the first musician awarded the Bharat Ratna.

**Terms explained**
- **Bhagavathalu** — the traditional male Brahmin performers of Kuchipudi.
- **Tarangam** — a Kuchipudi item danced on the rim of a brass plate.
- **Gharana** — a school/lineage of Hindustani music.
- **Raga / tala** — a melodic framework / a rhythmic cycle.

**Don't confuse**
- **Hindustani vs Carnatic** — Hindustani is northern and organised into gharanas; Carnatic is southern and shaped by the Trinity.
- **Siddhendra Yogi vs Bharata Muni** — Siddhendra Yogi shaped Kuchipudi; Bharata Muni wrote the all-India Natya Shastra.

**Remember it**
Carnatic Trinity = 'Tya-Di-Sha' (Tyagaraja, Dikshitar, Shyama Shastri); Kuchipudi = Siddhendra Yogi.

**TL;DR**
- Kuchipudi (AP) was shaped by Siddhendra Yogi; signature work Bhamakalapam, signature item Tarangam.
- Music splits into Hindustani (North) and Carnatic (South, incl. AP).
- Carnatic Trinity = Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, Shyama Shastri.
- M.S. Subbulakshmi was the first musician with a Bharat Ratna.
keyPoints: Kuchipudi (AP) shaped by Siddhendra Yogi; signature work Bhamakalapam
Kuchipudi's Tarangam = footwork on the rim of a brass plate; uses Vachika Abhinaya (dialogue)
Two classical music systems: Hindustani (North) and Carnatic (South, incl. AP)
Carnatic Trinity = Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, Shyama Shastri
Hindustani gharanas include Gwalior, Kirana, Agra, Jaipur, Patiala
M.S. Subbulakshmi was the first musician awarded the Bharat Ratna

items.title: Folk Arts, Crafts and Ancient Science
items.body:
### Folk arts, crafts and ancient science

**In one line**
India's folk arts and crafts (many from Andhra) and its ancient scientists and universities are grouped here as the 'culture and science' part of this topic.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC pairs a folk/craft form with its state and asks which scholar made which scientific contribution.

**The story**
Alongside the classical arts, every region kept living folk forms — shadow puppets, ballad-singers and painted cloth — with Andhra especially rich. In parallel, ancient India produced pioneering mathematicians, astronomers and physicians, taught at great residential universities that drew students from across Asia.

**Why it matters**
The AP folk/craft forms are state-weighted marks, and the scientists (zero, surgery) are favourite 'contribution' questions.

**Picture it**

| Scholar | Contribution |
|---|---|
| Aryabhata | decimal place-value, zero, value of π, eclipses by earth's rotation |
| Varahamihira | Brihat Samhita & Panchasiddhantika (astronomy/astrology) |
| Brahmagupta | rules for zero and negative numbers |
| Sushruta | surgery, including rhinoplasty |
| Charaka | medicine / Ayurveda |
| Atukuri Molla | a Telugu Ramayana (Molla Ramayanam), by a 16th-century potter-poet |

**Folk & crafts (AP-weighted):** puppetry — Tholu Bommalata (AP leather shadow puppets), Kathputli (Rajasthan strings); folk theatre — Burra Katha (AP ballad with tambura), Yakshagana (Karnataka), Jatra (Bengal), Tamasha (Maharashtra); crafts — Kalamkari (Srikalahasti/Machilipatnam, AP), Kondapalli & Etikoppaka toys (AP), Bidri work (Deccan). **Ancient universities:** Takshashila, Nalanda (Gupta/Pala patronage), Vikramshila, Valabhi.

**Terms explained**
- **Place-value system** — a way of writing numbers where a digit's position gives its value.
- **Rhinoplasty** — plastic surgery to reconstruct the nose.
- **Ayurveda** — the traditional Indian system of medicine.
- **Kalamkari** — hand-painted or block-printed cotton textile art.

**Don't confuse**
- **Aryabhata vs Brahmagupta** — Aryabhata gave place-value, zero and π; Brahmagupta gave the rules for using zero and negatives.
- **Sushruta vs Charaka** — Sushruta = surgery; Charaka = medicine/Ayurveda.

**Remember it**
'Sushruta cuts, Charaka cures' — surgery vs medicine.

**TL;DR**
- AP folk: Tholu Bommalata (puppets), Burra Katha (ballad); craft: Kalamkari, Kondapalli/Etikoppaka toys.
- Aryabhata: place-value, zero, π, earth's rotation; Brahmagupta: rules for zero/negatives.
- Sushruta = surgery (rhinoplasty); Charaka = Ayurveda.
- Ancient universities: Takshashila, Nalanda, Vikramshila, Valabhi.
keyPoints: Tholu Bommalata (leather shadow puppets) and Burra Katha are Andhra Pradesh folk forms
Kalamkari (Srikalahasti/Machilipatnam) is a hand-painted AP textile craft
Aryabhata: decimal place-value, zero, value of π, earth's rotation explaining eclipses
Varahamihira wrote Brihat Samhita and Panchasiddhantika (astronomy/astrology)
Brahmagupta framed rules for zero and negative numbers
Sushruta Samhita = surgery (incl. rhinoplasty); Charaka Samhita = medicine/Ayurveda
Ancient centres of learning: Takshashila, Nalanda, Vikramshila, Valabhi

items.title: More on Languages and Scripts — Detail
items.body:
### More on Languages and Scripts — Detail

**In one line**
The sub-groups of the language families, the classic text of each classical language, and the regional scripts.

**The story**
Indo-Aryan grew in three stages; the **Middle Indo-Aryan** stage of **Pali** (the **Tripitaka**), Prakrit (the **Jain Agamas**) and **Apabhramsha** led into modern Hindi, Bengali and Marathi — Apabhramsha being the **transitional** link. The Dravidian family has a northern branch (**Brahui**, Malto, Kurukh) and a central one (**Gondi**, Kui). The **Tibeto-Burman** branch covers Manipuri and Ladakhi, while **Ahom** has died out. Each classical language has its marker text: **Kavirajamarga** (Kannada), **Sarala Mahabharata** (Odia), **Dnyaneshwari** (Marathi), **Buranji**s (Assamese) and **Gaha Sattasai** of the Satavahana **Hala** (Prakrit). Status brings awards, **centres of excellence** and chairs. The Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages after the **92nd Amendment**. Scripts branched from Brahmi: the **Gupta script** into Nagari, **Tamil-Brahmi** in the south, **Grantha** for Sanskrit, **Sharada** in Kashmir and **Siddham**, which travelled to Tibet and Japan.

#### Languages and scripts

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Middle Indo-Aryan** | Prakrit, Pali, Apabhramsha (600 BCE–1000 CE) |
| **Apabhramsha** | Transitional stage to Modern Indo-Aryan |
| **Pali** | Language of the Buddhist Tripitaka |
| **Prakrit** | Language of the Jain Agamas |
| **Northern Dravidian** | Brahui, Malto, Kurukh |
| **Central Dravidian** | Gondi, Kui, Gadaba |
| **Tibeto-Burman** | Manipuri, Bhutia, Ladakhi, Sherpa |
| **Ahom** | Extinct Tai (Siamese-Chinese) language |
| **Kavirajamarga** | Classical Kannada (with Pampa Bharata) |
| **Sarala Mahabharata** | Classical Odia |
| **Dnyaneshwari** | Classical Marathi |
| **Gaha Sattasai** | Prakrit love poems of the Satavahana king Hala |
| **Buranjis** | Chronicles in Assamese |
| **Benefits of classical status** | Awards, centres of excellence, university chairs |
| **Eighth Schedule (22 languages)** | 92nd Amendment 2003 — Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali |
| **Gupta script** | Evolved into Nagari and Bengali |
| **Tamil-Brahmi** | Cave inscriptions and pottery (3rd c. BCE) |
| **Grantha** | Script for Sanskrit in the Tamil country |
| **Sharada** | Script of Kashmir |
| **Siddham** | Influenced Tibetan and Japanese scripts |

**Don't confuse**
- **Pali** = Buddhist canon; **Prakrit** = Jain canon.
- **Gaha Sattasai** (Hala, Satavahana — Andhra's own king) is a **Prakrit**, not Sanskrit, work.

**TL;DR**
- Middle Indo-Aryan: Pali (Tripitaka), Prakrit (Jain Agamas), Apabhramsha (transitional).
- Dravidian: Northern (Brahui), Central (Gondi); Tibeto-Burman: Manipuri; Ahom extinct.
- Classical texts: Kavirajamarga, Sarala Mahabharata, Dnyaneshwari, Buranjis, Gaha Sattasai (Hala).
- Scripts: Gupta → Nagari, Tamil-Brahmi, Grantha, Sharada (Kashmir), Siddham; 22 languages (92nd Amendment).
keyPoints: Brahui is a Northern Dravidian language.
Gaha Sattasai is a Prakrit work ascribed to the Satavahana king Hala.
Sharada was the script of Kashmir.
The 92nd Amendment (2003) added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali to the Eighth Schedule.

items.title: Sanskrit, Pali and Sangam Classics — Who Wrote What
items.body:
### Sanskrit, Pali and Sangam Classics — Who Wrote What

**In one line**
The author–work pairs from the Vedic texts to the medieval retellings that match-the-following questions draw on.

**The story**
Among Vedic texts the **Aitareya** Brahmana serves the Rigveda and the **Shatapatha** the Yajurveda; the **Brihadaranyaka** is the oldest Upanishad, and the **Mundaka** gave India its motto. Classical Sanskrit's great poems are **Bharavi**'s Kiratarjuniya and **Magha**'s Shishupala Vadha, besides Kalidasa's **Meghaduta**. Prose came from **Dandin** and **Banabhatta**, and drama from **Bhavabhuti**, **Vishakhadatta** and Harsha (**Nagananda**). The Buddhist poet **Ashvaghosha** wrote the Buddhacharita. Learning gave **Panini**'s grammar and **Amarasimha**'s lexicon. Fables came from **Vishnu Sharma** and the **Hitopadesha**. Regional retellings followed — **Kambar**'s Tamil Ramayana and Tulsidas's **Ramcharitmanas** — and Kerala's **Melpathur** wrote Narayaneeyam. The Sangam anthologies split into **Akananuru** (love) and **Purananuru** (war).

#### Author and work

### Persian, Urdu and Modern Indian Literature — Who Wrote What

**In one line**
The medieval chronicles and memoirs, and the modern novels and prizes that appear in author–work questions.

**The story**
Babur wrote in **Turkish**; **Jayasi** wrote Padmavat in Awadhi. Sultanate history comes from **Minhaj**, **Isami** and Amir Khusrau's **Khazain-ul-Futuh**. Foreign eyes gave **Al-Biruni**'s Kitab-ul-Hind and Ibn Battuta's **Rihla**, and Sufi talk the **Fawaid-ul-Fuad**. Dara Shikoh put the Upanishads into Persian as **Sirr-i-Akbar**. Guru Gobind Singh wrote the **Zafarnama**, and Ali Kufi the **Chachnama**. The modern age opens with Bankim's **Rajmohan's Wife** and **Anandamath**. Tagore won the Nobel in **1913**. Then came Premchand's **Godaan**, **Mulk Raj Anand**, Raja Rao's **Kanthapura**, **Samskara**, **Tamas** and **Kamayani**. Booker winners include **The God of Small Things** and **The White Tiger**.

items.title: Philosophy — Key Concepts and the Later Vedanta Schools
items.body:
### Philosophy — Key Concepts and the Later Vedanta Schools

**In one line**
The technical terms that separate the schools, and the three Bhakti-age Vedanta traditions beyond Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva.

**The story**
Philosophy in India is **darshana**, a '**vision**'; Madhavacharya's **Sarva Darshana Samgraha** summed the systems up. Life's aims are the four **purusharthas**, and its duties the three rinas (Guru, **Pitru**, Deva). Each school is known by its terms. Samkhya teaches **Satkaryavada**. Nyaya counts four means of knowledge, including **upamana**, and Mimamsa adds **Arthapatti**; its masters were **Kumarila Bhatta** and Prabhakara. Patanjali's eight limbs end in **samadhi**, and Vaisheshika builds the world from the **dravya**s. Among heterodox schools, the Charvakas admit only **four elements**. The Buddhists deny a self (**Anatta**), and the Jains teach **Syadvada** and split into **Digambara** and Svetambara. Later Vedanta added **Nimbarka**'s Dvaitadvaita, Vallabha's **Shuddhadvaita** and Chaitanya's **Achintya Bhedabheda**.

#### Concepts

| Term / school | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Darshana** | 'Intuitive vision' — philosophy |
| **Sarva Darshana Samgraha** | Madhavacharya (Vidyaranya) |
| **Three rinas** | Guru, Pitru and Deva rina |
| **Four purusharthas** | Dharma, Artha, Kama, Moksha |
| **Satkaryavada** | Samkhya — effect pre-exists in the cause |
| **Nyaya pramanas** | Four — incl. comparison (upamana) |
| **Mimamsa pramanas** | Adds Arthapatti and Anupalabdhi |
| **Kumarila Bhatta & Prabhakara** | Commentators of Mimamsa |
| **Ashtanga yoga** | Yama, niyama … dharana, dhyana, samadhi |
| **Vaisheshika dravyas** | Earth, water, fire, air, ether; atoms (anu) |
| **Charvaka** | Only perception; four elements; no soul or God |
| **Anatta** | Buddhist doctrine of no-self |
| **Syadvada** | Jain — truth relative to viewpoint |
| **Digambara** | Jain sect whose monks go unclothed |
| **Dvaitadvaita** | Nimbarka |
| **Shuddhadvaita** | Vallabhacharya |
| **Achintya Bhedabheda** | Chaitanya Mahaprabhu |

**Don't confuse**
- **Satkaryavada** (Samkhya — effect pre-exists) ≠ **Asatkaryavada** (Nyaya-Vaisheshika — effect is new).
- **Shuddhadvaita** = Vallabha; **Dvaitadvaita** = Nimbarka; **Vishishtadvaita** = Ramanuja.

**TL;DR**
- Darshana = vision; Sarva Darshana Samgraha (Madhavacharya); purusharthas; three rinas.
- Samkhya Satkaryavada; Nyaya 4 pramanas (upamana); Mimamsa (Arthapatti; Kumarila Bhatta).
- Yoga 8 limbs → samadhi; Vaisheshika dravyas; Charvaka four elements; Anatta; Syadvada; Digambara.
- Later Vedanta: Nimbarka (Dvaitadvaita), Vallabha (Shuddhadvaita), Chaitanya (Achintya Bhedabheda).
keyPoints: Satkaryavada is the Samkhya theory of causation.
Kumarila Bhatta was a commentator of Mimamsa.
Vallabhacharya taught Shuddhadvaita.
Nimbarka taught Dvaitadvaita.

items.title: Classical Dances — Gurus, Revivalists and Distinctive Terms
items.body:
### Classical Dances — Gurus, Revivalists and Distinctive Terms

**In one line**
For each of the nine forms: who revived it, who performs it, and the one technical term that identifies it.

**The story**
Dance theory beyond the Natya Shastra comes from Nandikeshvara's **Abhinaya Darpana**, and among the rasas **Bibhatsa** is disgust and **Bhayanaka** fear. **Rukmini Devi** brought Bharatanatyam to the stage; **Balasaraswati** kept the old style. **Leela Sokhey** revived Kathak. Its Lucknow gharana grew under **Wajid Ali Shah**, and **Janaki Prasad** founded the Banaras line; **Birju Maharaj** and **Sitara Devi** made it famous. **Vallathol** founded **Kalamandalam** for Kathakali, sung in **Manipravalam** to the **chenda**; **Kalamandalam Gopi** is its star. Odissi descends from the **Maharis** and uses the **tribhanga**; **Kelucharan Mohapatra** and **Sanjukta Panigrahi** revived it. Manipuri has the **Pung Cholom** and Guru **Bipin Singh**. Mohiniyattam's mother is **Kalyanikutty Amma**, and its alphabet the **atavukal**. Kuchipudi village was granted by **Tana Shah**; the dance uses **Tarakas**. Sattriya grew from the **Ankia Naat** and its **Paurashik** style; it became classical in **2000**. **Mayurbhanj** Chhau is maskless, and **Chhau** entered the UNESCO list in **2010**.

| **Maharis** | Temple dancers behind Odissi |

| **Chhau — UNESCO** | Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2010 |

**Don't confuse**
- **Mayurbhanj Chhau** has **no masks**; Purulia and Seraikella Chhau use masks.
- **Vallathol** revived Kathakali (and Mohiniyattam); **Rukmini Devi** revived Bharatanatyam; **Leela Sokhey** revived Kathak.
- The source PDF writes 'V.N. Menon' — the poet **Vallathol Narayana Menon**.

**TL;DR**
- Abhinaya Darpana (Nandikeshvara); rasas Bibhatsa (disgust), Bhayanaka (fear).
- Bharatanatyam: Rukmini Devi (Kalakshetra), Balasaraswati; Kathak: Leela Sokhey, Lucknow (Wajid Ali Shah), Banaras (Janaki Prasad), Birju Maharaj, Sitara Devi.
- Kathakali/Mohiniyattam: Vallathol, Kalamandalam, Manipravalam, chenda, Kalyanikutty Amma, atavukal; Odissi: Maharis, tribhanga, Kelucharan.
- Manipuri: Pung Cholom, Bipin Singh; Kuchipudi: Tana Shah grant 1678, tarakas; Sattriya: Ankia Naat, 2000; Chhau: Mayurbhanj no masks, UNESCO 2010.
keyPoints: Rukmini Devi Arundale founded Kalakshetra.

### Folk Dances by State

**In one line**
The state-wise list examiners match — with Andhra's own Dhimsa, Veeranatyam and Kolattam first.

**The story**
Folk dances come from local life, not the Natya Shastra. Andhra Pradesh has the tribal **Dhimsa**, the Shaiva **Veeranatyam** and the stick dance **Kolattam**. Haryana has **Saang** and **Dhamal**, Himachal the **Nati**, and Jharkhand **Karam**. Karnataka has **Dollu Kunitha** and **Huli Vesha**; Kerala **Theyyam** and **Ottamthullal**. Madhya Pradesh has **Matki**, Maharashtra **Lavani** and **Koli**, and Manipur **Thang Ta**. Odisha has **Gotipua** and **Dalkhai**, and Punjab **Gidda**. Rajasthan has **Kalbeliya**, **Bhavai** and **Kachchhi Ghodi**; Tamil Nadu **Karagattam** and **Mayil Attam**. Gujarat has **Garba** and Assam **Bihu**.

items.body:
### Music — Gharanas, Singers, Instrument Classes and Folk Songs

**In one line**
The founder or star of each gharana, the Carnatic landmarks, the four instrument classes and the state folk-song forms.

**The story**
Hindustani khayal is organised by gharana. **Gwalior** (Nathan Peerbaksh) is the oldest, and **Bade Ghulam Ali Khan** made Patiala famous. Kirana gave **Bhimsen Joshi**; **Mewati** gave Pandit Jasraj. **Alladiya Khan** founded Jaipur-Atrauli, and **Faiyaz Khan** led Agra; **Sahaswan** produced Rashid Khan. **Dhrupad** survives in the Gundechas. Begum Akhtar was the **Mallika-e-Ghazal**, and Amir Khusrau, disciple of **Nizamuddin Auliya**, shaped qawwali. Carnatic music begins with **Purandara Dasa** and its forms **Varnam** and kriti. The **Tanjore Quartet** set Bharatanatyam's music, and **Pattammal** and MS were in the female trinity. The Natya Shastra classes instruments into four, the drums being **avanaddha**. Folk song is regional: **Baul** and **Bhatiali** in Bengal, **Powada** in Maharashtra, **Kajri** in UP, **Mando** in Goa, **Villu Pattu** in Tamil Nadu, **Maand** in Rajasthan, and Pandavani by **Teejan Bai**.

items.title: Theatre and Puppetry by State
items.body:
### Theatre and Puppetry by State

**In one line**
From the earliest cave theatres to every state folk-theatre form and the four kinds of puppets.

**The story**
India's oldest stages may be the **Sitabenga** and Jogimara caves. Sanskrit drama was **Lokadharmi** or natyadharmi, and Kerala keeps it alive in **Koodiyattam**. UNESCO also lists **Ramman** and **Mudiyettu**. Each state has a folk theatre: **Jatra** (Bengal), **Bhavai** (Gujarat), **Nautanki** (UP), **Swang** (Haryana) and **Maach** (MP). Kashmir has **Bhand Pather**, Tamil Nadu **Therukoothu** and Kerala **Krishnattam**. The Konkan has **Dashavatar**, Assam **Oja-Pali** and Andhra **Pagati Vesh**alu. The state backed them through the Sangeet Natak Akademi (**1952**). Puppetry comes in four kinds. String puppets include **Bommalattam**, **Gombeyatta**, **Kundhei** and **Kalasutri**. Shadow puppets include **Togalu** Gombeyatta and **Ravanachhaya**. Rod puppets include **Putul Nach** and **Yampuri**, and glove puppets **Pavakoothu**. **Meher Contractor** brought modern puppetry.

| **Sitabenga & Jogimara caves** | Among the oldest amphitheatres |

### Handicrafts of India by State

**In one line**
Textiles, metal, glass, terracotta, leather, wood, toys, stone and floor art — the craft-to-state pairs.

**The story**
Textiles first: **Bandhani** tie-dye of Rajasthan, Lucknow's **Chikankari**, Bengal's **Kantha** and Punjab's **Phulkari**. Odisha has **Pipli** appliqué and Gujarat **Patola** double ikat. The Nilgiris have **Toda** embroidery, MP **Chanderi** and Bihar **Bhagalpur** tussar. **Firozabad** makes bangles and **Bankura** terracotta horses. Metalwork includes **Bidri** inlay, **Dokra** lost-wax casting, Telangana's **Pembarthi** sheet metal and Rajasthan's **Marori** etching. In leather, Maharashtra has **Kolhapuri** chappals and Bikaner **Manoti** art. Kashmir has **Khatamband** ceilings, **Channapatna** is the toy town and Assam makes **Pith** dolls. **Makrana** gave the Taj its marble. Floors are decorated with **Mandana** in Rajasthan and **Muggulu** in Andhra.

|---|---|
| **Bandhani** | Rajasthan / Gujarat tie-and-dye |

| **Mandana** | Rajasthan / MP floor art |
| **Muggulu** | Andhra name for kolam floor art |

**Don't confuse**
- **Bidri** = Bidar (Karnataka; now also Telangana GI); **Pembarthi** = Telangana; AP's own crafts (Kondapalli, Etikoppaka, Kalamkari, Budithi) are in the AP-culture notes.
- **Patola** (Gujarat) is double ikat; **Pochampally** (Telangana) is single ikat.

**TL;DR**
- Textiles: Bandhani, Chikankari, Kantha, Phulkari, Pipli, Patola, Toda, Chanderi, Bhagalpur.
- Glass/clay/metal: Firozabad, Bankura, Bidri, Dokra, Pembarthi, Marori.
- Leather/wood/toys: Kolhapuri, Manoti, Khatamband, Channapatna, pith dolls.
- Stone/floor: Makrana marble; Mandana; Muggulu (AP).

items.body:
### Ancient Science, Mathematics and Universities — Detail

**In one line**
The book behind each scientist, the metallurgists and physicians, and who founded each great university.

**The story**
Mathematics runs from **Baudhayana**'s Sulbasutra and **Pingala**'s metres to the **Aryabhatiya** (499), the **Brahmasphutasiddhanta** (628), Bhaskara's **Lilavati** and the infinite series of Madhava of **Sangamagrama**. Chemistry and metallurgy appear in Nagarjuna's **Rasaratnakara**. Medicine has Charaka, physician to **Kanishka**, and Vagbhata's **Ashtanga Hridaya**. Learning had great centres: Nalanda (**Kumaragupta I**), Vikramashila (**Dharmapala**), **Odantapuri** and **Maitraka** Valabhi. Astronomy returned in stone with Sawai **Jai Singh**'s five observatories.

#### Science

| Work / centre | Author / founder |
|---|---|
| **Aryabhatiya** | Aryabhata (499 CE) |
| **Brahmasphutasiddhanta** | Brahmagupta (628 CE) |
| **Lilavati** | Bhaskara II |
| **Baudhayana Sulbasutra** | Statement of the 'Pythagoras' theorem |
| **Chandahshastra** | Pingala — binary-like metres |
| **Rasaratnakara** | Nagarjuna — metallurgy, zinc distillation |
| **Ashtanga Hridaya** | Vagbhata |
| **Madhava of Sangamagrama** | Kerala school — infinite series |
| **Charaka** | Physician of Kanishka (Charaka Samhita) |
| **Nalanda** | Founded by Kumaragupta I |
| **Vikramashila** | Pala king Dharmapala |
| **Odantapuri** | Pala king Gopala |
| **Valabhi** | Maitraka university (Gujarat) |
| **Jantar Mantar observatories** | Sawai Jai Singh II (five) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Brahmagupta** = Brahmasphutasiddhanta (rules for zero); **Aryabhata** = Aryabhatiya (place value, π); **Bhaskara II** = Lilavati.
- **Nalanda** = Kumaragupta I (Gupta); **Vikramashila** = Dharmapala (Pala).

**TL;DR**
- Aryabhatiya 499; Brahmasphutasiddhanta 628; Lilavati (Bhaskara II); Baudhayana; Pingala; Madhava of Sangamagrama.
- Nagarjuna's Rasaratnakara; Vagbhata; Charaka (Kanishka).
- Universities: Nalanda (Kumaragupta I), Vikramashila (Dharmapala), Odantapuri (Gopala), Valabhi (Maitrakas).
- Jantar Mantar: Sawai Jai Singh II.
keyPoints: Lilavati was written by Bhaskara II.
Vikramashila was founded by Dharmapala.
Nalanda was founded by Kumaragupta I.
Nagarjuna's Rasaratnakara describes zinc distillation.

### For Mains — Literature, Science & Culture

**In one line**
For Mains Paper-II (M2-1b and M2-2b), treat India's literature, philosophy and science as evidence of continuity, plurality and the AP contribution to Telugu culture.

**How Mains frames this topic**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Plurality | Sanskrit, Tamil Sangam, Persian/Urdu and Telugu streams coexisting |
| Continuity | Natya Shastra → living classical dance; Brahmi → modern scripts |
| Significance | science (zero, surgery, π) shaping world knowledge; universities as soft power |
| Patronage | Vijayanagara golden age; court vs non-court (Molla, Vemana) voices |
| AP angle | Kuchipudi, Kavitrayam, Nalanda-type learning, Amaravati Buddhist scholarship |
| Way forward | classical-language funding, manuscript conservation, intangible-heritage protection |

**Data points / examples to quote**
- Classical-language years: Tamil 2004, Telugu 2008, Pali/Prakrit/Marathi 2024.
- Aryabhata (place-value, zero, π) and Brahmagupta (rules for zero/negatives).
- Ancient universities: Takshashila, Nalanda, Vikramshila, Valabhi.
- Telugu: Kavitrayam, Krishnadevaraya's Amuktamalyada, Peddana's Manucharitra.

**Use in answers**
- Open by naming the four literary streams, then argue 'unity in grammar, diversity in expression' for dance.
- Diagram idea: a 2x3 grid of streams (Sanskrit/Tamil/Persian/Telugu) × dimensions (works/authors/significance).
- Quote: the Tirukkural's universal ethics, or 'India gave the world the zero'.
- Close an AP-flavoured answer with Kuchipudi, the Kavitrayam and Nagarjunakonda's Buddhist learning.

**TL;DR**
- Argue plurality → continuity → significance → patronage → AP angle → conservation.
- Keep anchors ready: classical-language years, Aryabhata/Brahmagupta, Nalanda, Telugu golden age.
- Reliable thesis: 'Indian culture is a continuous, plural tradition sustained by patronage'.
keyPoints: Mains clauses M2-1b / M2-2b (Paper-II) — literature, fine arts and science; frame as plurality + continuity.
Structure answers as plurality → continuity → significance → patronage → AP angle → conservation.
Quote anchors: classical-language years, Aryabhata/Brahmagupta, Nalanda-type universities.
AP angle: Kuchipudi, the Kavitrayam, Krishnadevaraya's golden age, Nagarjunakonda Buddhist learning.
